Title: Fünf Landtagswahlen 2026: Wie die Bürgerinnen und Bürger wählen würden

Summary: 
According to a report by rnd.de published on March 03, 2026, five state parliament elections (Landtagswahlen) are scheduled in Germany for 2026, with current polls indicating a potential fundamental shift in the balance of political power. 

In Baden-Württemberg, the upcoming election is set for March 8, 2026. Following the 2021 results where the Greens won 32.6% of the vote and the CDU 24.1%, the current coalition led by 77-year-old Minister President Winfried Kretschmann (the first and only Green party leader in this role since 2011) is ending as Kretschmann is not running again. Polls show the Greens have lost significant support, while the AfD has gained; however, all major parties rule out a coalition with the AfD and its candidate Markus Frohnmaier. Cem Özdemir (Greens) and Manuel Hagel (CDU) are the leading candidates to succeed Kretschmann.

In Rhineland-Palatinate, the election is on March 22, 2026. The SPD has governed continuously since 1991, currently in a coalition with the Greens and FDP for nine years under Minister President Alexander Schweitzer, who took office in July 2024 replacing Malu Dreyer. The six parties represented are SPD, CDU, Greens, AfD, FDP, and Freie Wähler. Polls suggest the SPD's long reign is ending as the CDU leads and the AfD has gained the most ground, leaving the current 'traffic light' coalition without a majority. Gordon Schnieder (CDU), Katrin Eder (Greens), and Jan Bollinger (AfD) are the respective top candidates.

In Saxony-Anhalt, the election is scheduled for September 6, 2026. The 2021 election saw the CDU win 37.1% and the AfD 20.8%, leading to a 'Germany Coalition' (CDU, SPD, FDP) under Minister President Reiner Haseloff (CDU). Current polls show the AfD leading significantly, with an absolute majority possible if other parties fail to clear the 5% threshold. Haseloff is not running again, and CDU candidate Sven Schulze has rejected cooperation with the AfD.

In Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the election is also on September 6, 2026. The 2021 election was won by the SPD with 39.6%, followed by the AfD with 16.7%, leading to a coalition between the SPD and The Left. The current 'red-red' government under Minister President Manuela Schwesig faces a difficult situation; polls indicate no majority and a significant lead for the AfD. The SPD could lose half its votes following a national downward trend. Leif-Erik Holm, a former radio host and Bundestag member, is the AfD's top candidate.

In Berlin, a repeat election is set for September 20, 2026, following the invalid 2023 vote caused by missing ballot papers and long wait times. The 2023 repeat election saw the CDU win 28.2% under Kai Wegner, forming a coalition with the SPD despite the previous red-green-red majority. Current polls show the CDU leading, with the Left, AfD, Greens, and SPD closely behind. A two-party coalition is no longer possible, and only three-party alliances are mathematically feasible, with a 'red-red-green' coalition potentially possible if the SPD and Left reunite.

Following the 2021 results where the Greens won 32.6% of the vote and the CDU 24.1%, the current coalition led by 77-year-old Minister President Winfried Kretschmann (the first and only Green party leader in this role since 2011) is ending as Kretschmann is not running again. Polls show the Greens have lost significant support, while the AfD has gained; however, all major parties rule out a coalition with the AfD and its candidate Markus Frohnmaier. Cem Özdemir (Greens) and Manuel Hagel (CDU) are the leading candidates to succeed Kretschmann.

In Rhineland-Palatinate, the election is on March 22, 2026. The SPD has governed continuously since 1991, currently in a coalition with the Greens and FDP for nine years under Minister President Alexander Schweitzer, who took office in July 2024 replacing Malu Dreyer. The six parties represented are SPD, CDU, Greens, AfD, FDP, and Freie Wähler. Polls suggest the SPD's long reign is ending as the CDU leads and the AfD has gained the most ground, leaving the current 'traffic light' coalition without a majority. Gordon Schnieder (CDU), Katrin Eder (Greens), and Jan Bollinger (AfD) are the respective top candidates.

In Saxony-Anhalt, the election is scheduled for September 6, 2026. The 2021 election saw the CDU win 37.1% and the AfD 20.8%, leading to a 'Germany Coalition' (CDU, SPD, FDP) under Minister President Reiner Haseloff (CDU). Current polls show the AfD leading significantly, with an absolute majority possible if other parties fail to clear the 5% threshold. Haseloff is not running again, and CDU candidate Sven Schulze has rejected cooperation with the AfD.

In Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the election is also on September 6, 2026. The 2021 election was won by the SPD with 39.6%, followed by the AfD with 16.7%, leading to a coalition between the SPD and The Left. The current 'red-red' government under Minister President Manuela Schwesig faces a difficult situation; polls indicate no majority and a significant lead for the AfD. The SPD could lose half its votes following a national downward trend. Leif-Erik Holm, a former radio host and Bundestag member, is the AfD's top candidate.

In Berlin, a repeat election is set for September 20, 2026, following the invalid 2023 vote caused by missing ballot papers and long wait times. The 2023 repeat election saw the CDU win 28.2% under Kai Wegner, forming a coalition with the SPD despite the previous red-green-red majority. Current polls show the CDU leading, with the Left, AfD, Greens, and SPD closely behind. A two-party coalition is no longer possible, and only three-party alliances are mathematically feasible, with a 'red-red-green' coalition potentially possible if the SPD and Left reunite.

articles.title: AfD Launches Election Campaign Targeting Rhineland-Palatinate Interior Minister
articles.summary: The AfD in Rhineland-Palatinate has launched a targeted election campaign ahead of the March 22, 2026, state parliamentary election, focusing on criticism of Innenminister Michael Ebling (SPD). The campaign centers on demands for stricter checks on constitutional loyalty, including enhanced vetting for public sector employment and background checks for staff in parliamentary factions. The AfD accuses Ebling of leading a 'crusade' against the party and its members. A key point of contention is a government list identifying over 100 groups as extremist—such as Al-Qaeda, the Reichsbürger movement, the Muslim Brotherhood, and the KPD—under the state’s tightened 'Verfassungstreue' (constitutional loyalty) regulations. The campaign, officially launched on Friday in Idar-Oberstein with national leaders Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla, includes a dedicated website featuring a satirical 'State Office for Opposition Suppression' where supporters can take a fictional 'ideological test.' The AfD aims for a result of 20 percent plus X, with the campaign slogan 'We will handle it.'

articles.title: State Elections 2026: Current Polling Data in Baden-Württemberg and Key Federal States
articles.summary: According to recent polling data from February 2026, the Christian Democratic Union (CDU) leads in Baden-Württemberg with an average of 29 percent support, followed by the Greens and the AfD, with the Greens having narrowed the gap slightly in recent months. The data includes a margin of error: at 30 percent support, the actual value could vary by up to ±3 percentage points. The distribution of seats in the state parliament is projected using a 'Five-Percent Scenario,' where parties below the 5 percent threshold would be excluded, redistributing their potential seats. In Rhineland-Palatinate, the CDU is projected to be the strongest party, followed by the SPD and AfD, with the FDP, BSW, and Free Voters hovering near the 4 percent threshold and the Left Party at 6 percent—just above the 5 percent hurdle. In Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the AfD leads significantly ahead of the SPD, CDU, and Left Party, though the Greens may fall below the 5 percent threshold. In Berlin, the CDU leads the SPD and AfD, with Mayor Kai Wegner potentially retaining his position despite criticism over the January power outage; however, BSW and FDP are projected to fall short of the 5 percent threshold. In Saxony-Anhalt, the AfD leads the CDU and Left Party, and if it surpasses 40 percent, it could achieve an absolute majority. A central question ahead of the 2026 state elections is the AfD’s performance, particularly given its classification as right-extremist in parts of the political spectrum. The AfD is projected to be the strongest party in both Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, as indicated by color-coded highlights in the accompanying graphic.
